questions.explanation: Long cases make patients restless, which prompts more drug and raises the chance of deeper-than-intended sedation. Consider whether discomfort, position, or a full bladder is the real cause.

questions.stem: Deep sedation is requested for a prone patient whose airway would be difficult to access. What is the safest planning response?
options: Reconsider whether a secured airway/general anesthetic offers a safer rescue profile
Proceed because pulse oximetry will identify problems early enough
Assume the patient can be rapidly turned supine during any emergency
questions.explanation: Prone positioning makes airway access difficult. A secured airway or GA may be safer than deep sedation.

questions.stem: A laterally positioned patient under MAC develops mild hypoxemia. Which mechanical change can contribute?
options: Reduced FRC/compliance in the dependent lung
Improved oxygen reserve in both lungs
questions.explanation: In the lateral position, the dependent lung loses compliance and FRC, worsening gas exchange.

questions.stem: Why is postoperative visual loss emphasized despite its low incidence after prolonged prone surgery?
options: The injury is rare but potentially permanent and devastating
It is common but always reversible
It occurs mainly after brief supine cases
It is caused only by direct eye pressure
questions.explanation: Postoperative visual loss is rare but can be permanent, which is why prevention matters.

questions.stem: Which common procedure most often pairs a very brief but intense stimulus with a need for rapid recovery?
options: Superficial abscess drainage with adequate local anesthesia
questions.explanation: Cardioversion is usually brief deep sedation because the shock is intensely stimulating. The others are usually manageable at lighter depths.

questions.stem: During colonoscopy under deep sedation, forceful external abdominal pressure is applied while protective reflexes are depressed. Which risk may increase?
questions.explanation: External abdominal pressure can push gastric contents upward while the airway is unprotected.

questions.stem: When planning procedural sedation, which question best predicts peak analgesic requirement?
options: How intense and variable will the noxious stimulation be?
How many staff are in the room?
What oxygen flow rate will be used?
questions.explanation: The intensity and variability of stimulation determine how much sedation and analgesia are needed.

questions.stem: Why can carpal-tunnel release often be performed with effective local anesthesia and only minimal systemic sedation?
options: Adequate local anesthesia can blunt the procedural nociceptive input, reducing the need for systemic drugs
The procedure requires intense variable stimulation despite local anesthesia
The airway is shared with the surgeon
questions.explanation: Effective local anesthesia makes stimulation low, so minimal sedation is enough.

questions.stem: Why does MRI sedation demand special rescue planning even though the scan itself is painless?
options: The remote environment, scanner bore, and MRI-compatibility constraints can delay physical access and airway rescue
Monitoring is unnecessary because no incision occurs
questions.explanation: MRI suites are remote, the bore limits airway access, and only MRI-compatible equipment can be used, which slows rescue.

questions.stem: A supine patient with severe OSA repeatedly obstructs during sedation. Which positional adjustment may improve upper-airway patency if the procedure permits?
questions.explanation: Supine positioning lets the tongue and soft tissue fall back, worsening OSA obstruction. Lateral or semi-upright positions improve airway patency.

questions.stem: During sedated TEE, hypoxemia develops and airway maneuvers are difficult. Which procedural factor contributes directly?
options: The probe occupies the pharyngeal space and may impede airway access until withdrawn
The patient must perform neurologic testing
questions.explanation: During TEE, the probe occupies the pharynx and esophagus, limiting airway access; it may need to be removed to manage the airway.

questions.stem: A procedure alternates between minimal stimulation and brief intense pain. What is the principal titration challenge?
options: Drug effect may outlast the painful stimulus, causing oversedation when stimulation suddenly falls
The deepest required level should be maintained throughout
Changing stimulation affects analgesia but never sedation depth
questions.explanation: Variable stimulation means the right depth changes moment to moment, so titrate carefully.

questions.stem: During beach-chair MAC, a patient becomes confused with arm BP 92/54 mmHg. Which explanation should be considered urgently?
options: Cerebral perfusion pressure at head level may be inadequate despite the arm-cuff value
Upright positioning guarantees adequate cerebral perfusion
Dependent-lung collapse is the only likely cause
Direct eye pressure is causing the confusion
questions.explanation: Beach chair positioning alters cerebral autoregulation. With the cuff at the arm, brain perfusion pressure is lower than the reading, so confusion is a warning sign.

questions.stem: Why must position be considered during MAC even when no airway device is planned?
options: Position can alter airway patency, rescue access, ventilation, and perfusion
Position matters only during general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Position affects airway patency, access for rescue, and physiology such as cerebral perfusion and FRC.

questions.stem: A lateral-position patient under MAC develops mild desaturation without obvious obstruction. Which positional physiology may contribute?
questions.explanation: Lateral positioning lowers FRC and compliance in the dependent lung, reducing oxygen reserve.

questions.stem: Which patient/procedure combination increases postoperative visual-loss risk during a prolonged prone operation?
options: Obesity/vascular disease combined with prolonged duration, blood loss, or anemia
Young age with normal hemoglobin and short duration
Normal perfusion and no eye pressure
questions.explanation: Obesity, vascular disease, anemia, blood loss, and prolonged surgery are POVL risk factors.

questions.stem: Why is it incorrect to treat MAC as a fixed depth between moderate and deep sedation?
options: MAC describes an anesthesia service and preparedness, not a single sedation depth
MAC is synonymous with deep sedation
questions.explanation: MAC describes a service by an anesthesia professional and can range from minimal sedation to GA. Depth does not define it.

questions.stem: During MAC, a propofol bolus briefly makes the patient unresponsive and ventilation requires support. Does the label MAC itself cease to apply solely because depth changed?
options: No; MAC is the anesthesia service, while the patient may transiently enter deeper sedation or general anesthesia requiring rescue
Yes; MAC ends whenever verbal responsiveness is lost
Yes; the case automatically becomes nurse-administered moderate sedation
No; because MAC cannot include airway intervention
questions.explanation: MAC is defined by the anesthesia service, not depth, and can range up to GA while the provider is prepared to manage it.

questions.stem: Why is credentialing for nurse-administered moderate sedation not equivalent to providing MAC?
options: MAC is an anesthesia service requiring an anesthesia professional prepared for deeper anesthesia, airway rescue, and conversion to general anesthesia
Both roles are identical if propofol is not used
Moderate-sedation credentials automatically authorize general anesthesia
questions.explanation: MAC must be provided by a qualified anesthesia professional prepared to manage the airway and physiologic changes, including conversion to GA.

questions.stem: Which THREE components are part of the MAC anesthesia service? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: MAC includes preprocedure evaluation, intraprocedure care, and postprocedure management, the same scope as other anesthetics.

questions.stem: Which medication strategy can be part of MAC when appropriate to the procedure and patient?
options: A tailored combination of anxiolytic, hypnotic, analgesic, and/or amnestic drugs with local/regional anesthesia as applicable
Neuromuscular blockade solely to keep an unsecured-airway patient still
Benzodiazepines and opioids are the only permissible agents
questions.explanation: MAC may use anxiolytic, hypnotic, analgesic, and amnestic drugs, alone or with local or regional anesthesia.

questions.stem: During MAC, a field block fails; severe pain persists, and attempts to deepen sedation repeatedly cause obstruction. What should the anesthesia provider be prepared to do?
options: Change the anesthetic plan, including conversion to general anesthesia with a secured airway when needed
Continue escalating propofol despite recurrent obstruction
Use neuromuscular blockade without securing the airway
Ignore pain until the procedure ends
questions.explanation: MAC requires readiness to convert to GA when the procedure cannot proceed safely, as with a failed block and obstruction.

questions.stem: A facility proposes skipping the airway assessment because a patient is scheduled for MAC rather than general anesthesia. What is the key flaw?
options: MAC requires preanesthetic evaluation and readiness for airway rescue/conversion because depth can change
Airway assessment is relevant only when intubation is planned
MAC cannot progress to general anesthesia
Only the proceduralist needs to assess the airway
questions.explanation: Because MAC can progress to GA, its evaluation and monitoring standards are comparable to GA, including the airway exam.

questions.stem: Absolute immobility is required for a procedure despite adequate analgesia. Which capability can general anesthesia provide that routine MAC cannot safely guarantee?
options: Controlled immobility including neuromuscular blockade with a secured anesthetic plan when indicated
questions.explanation: MAC provides sedation and amnesia, but the patient can still move. GA can include neuromuscular blocking drugs.

questions.stem: What fundamentally distinguishes intended moderate sedation from an anesthesia-provider MAC service?
options: Moderate sedation targets preserved purposeful responsiveness, whereas MAC is a broader anesthesia service prepared for changing depth and rescue/conversion
MAC is always deeper than moderate sedation
Moderate sedation requires an anesthesia professional in every case
MAC excludes local or regional anesthesia
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation keeps purposeful response; MAC can go deeper and includes readiness to convert to GA.

questions.stem: During a stable 3-hour MAC, the anesthesia provider leaves the room for 20 minutes and the patient becomes apneic. Which standard was violated?
options: Presence required at induction and emergence, with phone contact between
Presence required during conversion to GA
Presence required for ASA IV patients
questions.explanation: MAC requires continuous presence of the anesthesia team, because depth can change at any time.

questions.stem: Which item is NOT a routine ASA requirement for MAC?
questions.explanation: MAC requirements include preanesthesia evaluation, a qualified provider, continuous monitoring, airway management, conversion to GA, and postanesthesia care. Arterial lines depend on the patient.

questions.stem: Which FIVE elements belong in a facility policy for MAC? (Select 5)
options: Develop and document an anesthetic plan
Be prepared to convert to GA
Have a qualified anesthesia professional present
Have airway management equipment immediately available
questions.explanation: ASA requires a documented plan, readiness to convert, a qualified provider present, airway equipment, and postanesthesia monitoring.

questions.stem: A MAC patient obstructs, but the only airway equipment in the room is a nasal cannula and suction. Which requirement was violated?
options: Airway equipment and ability to provide ventilatory support must be immediately available
A code team must be paged before MAC begins so they can respond to problems
The patient must be intubated before MAC
A nasal cannula and suction are sufficient for MAC
questions.explanation: MAC requires immediate availability of airway equipment and the ability to provide ventilatory support.

questions.stem: After MAC, a drowsy patient is sent directly toward discharge without monitored recovery. Which standard is being missed?
options: Discharge once the patient can walk
Recording vital signs at discharge once the patient can walk
Discharge once the patient is awake and talking
questions.explanation: MAC requires postanesthesia care with monitoring, assessment, and documentation, like any anesthetic.

questions.stem: A MAC preop note includes only procedure, NPO status, and allergies despite OSA, GERD, and prior difficult intubation. What important assessment is missing?
options: History, medications, airway assessment, and aspiration risk
A recent ECG and chest X-ray
A repeat chest X-ray and CBC
The surgeon's operative plan and the expected length of the procedure
questions.explanation: The MAC preanesthesia evaluation includes history, medications, allergies, airway, and aspiration risk; this patient's OSA, GERD, and airway history are critical.

questions.stem: A propofol infusion is planned, but no infusion pump is available. What should be done before starting MAC?
options: Obtain an infusion pump for the continuous agent
Run propofol by gravity and count drops
Give intermittent boluses instead of an infusion
Give propofol as intermittent boluses instead
questions.explanation: Infusion pumps are part of the MAC environment when continuous agents are used; gravity delivery is unreliable.

questions.stem: Why does a crowded remote-procedure room with equipment blocking the head increase MAC risk?
options: Procedural equipment and remote sites can limit airway access
It matters mainly in the main OR, where staff are close by
It limits the surgeon's sterile field
questions.explanation: Workspace and equipment can limit airway access, especially in remote locations.

questions.stem: A sedation nurse is asked to deliver propofol for TAVR while the interventionalist works. What is the core problem?
options: MAC with propofol requires an anesthesia provider able to rescue the airway
Nothing, since the nurse is credentialed in moderate sedation
The cardiologist should give the propofol himself while performing the TAVR
A respiratory therapist should give the propofol
questions.explanation: MAC is provided by an anesthesia provider capable of airway rescue and converting to GA.

questions.stem: Why can light sedation still be considered MAC when delivered by an anesthesia professional?
options: The nurse, because MAC is defined by the service, not depth
The colleague, because MAC means deep sedation
Both, since MAC depends on both the depth and the provider
questions.explanation: MAC describes the anesthesia service provided, not how deep the patient is.

questions.stem: Which scenario most clearly represents MAC rather than nurse-administered moderate sedation?
options: A CRNA manages sedation and is ready to convert to GA
A nurse gives midazolam and fentanyl per protocol
An endoscopist gives propofol while scoping
A patient takes oral anxiolysis before an MRI
questions.explanation: MAC is delivered by an anesthesia provider with readiness to convert to GA.

questions.stem: During MAC, agitation and coughing prevent the procedure from continuing safely. What should the anesthesia provider be prepared to do?
options: Be prepared to convert when clinically necessary
Convert when the surgeon requests it
Convert after the procedure is finished so the surgeon is not interrupted
questions.explanation: ASA requires readiness to convert to GA whenever it is clinically necessary.

questions.stem: A remote endoscopy room lacks capnography, positive-pressure ventilation equipment, and emergency drugs. Which THREE must be added? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The MAC environment requires oxygen, suction, ventilation equipment, physiologic monitoring with capnography, emergency drugs, and airway equipment.

questions.stem: A patient briefly becomes unresponsive to voice during cataract MAC. Does that alone mean the case is no longer MAC?
options: Yes, MAC is a service that can include deeper levels
No, the service must now be billed as GA
No, because MAC is limited to moderate sedation by definition
Yes, as long as the patient responds to pain
questions.explanation: MAC remains the service even when depth varies. The provider must manage the deeper state and be ready to convert.

questions.stem: A facility wants to omit airway exams for healthy MAC patients. What standard applies?
options: The MAC preop evaluation should be as comprehensive as for GA
A brief evaluation is acceptable for ASA I–II
The airway exam is needed for ASA III or higher patients
The airway exam is needed when deep sedation is planned
questions.explanation: Because any MAC patient may need conversion to GA, the preop evaluation should be as comprehensive as for GA.

questions.stem: Monitors and sedatives are ready for MAC, but no laryngoscope, ETT, or induction plan has been identified. What is missing?
options: A plan for conversion to GA
questions.explanation: A conversion-to-GA plan with equipment and drugs must be developed before starting MAC.

questions.stem: Which FIVE patient factors substantially increase MAC risk? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: Important MAC risk conditions include severe cardiovascular disease, pulmonary hypertension, OSA, morbid obesity, renal or hepatic disease, chronic opioid use, and advanced age.

questions.stem: Why does inability to tolerate a long painful position increase risk during MAC?
options: Intolerance leads to movement, which prompts more sedation and airway risk
Position tolerance affects surgical exposure more than sedation
Position tolerance determines which PACU bay the patient will go to afterward
questions.explanation: If a patient cannot tolerate position or duration, she moves and becomes restless, which leads to deeper sedation with an unsecured airway. That may favor GA.

questions.stem: Which planned position most strongly increases concern about losing airway access during MAC?
options: Prone positioning with the head turned away from you
Supine positioning with the face uncovered
A short procedure in the semi-upright position
A lateral position with the face visible
questions.explanation: Prone positioning with the head turned away makes it hard to reach and manage the airway, so plan for loss of access.

questions.stem: A regional block is combined with propofol sedation administered by a CRNA. How is the anesthetic best classified?
options: MAC, which can accompany regional anesthesia
Regional anesthesia alone, since a block was placed
Moderate sedation, since the patient was arousable
questions.explanation: MAC can be combined with local or regional anesthesia and is defined by the anesthesia service.

questions.stem: A patient remains drowsy and hypoventilates after light propofol MAC. What recovery requirement still applies?
options: MAC requires postanesthesia care with monitoring like other anesthetics
Phase 2 recovery is enough after light propofol sedation
PACU is needed after GA but not after MAC
PACU is needed if the patient also received an opioid during the case
questions.explanation: MAC patients usually go to some form of PACU for monitoring and assessment, especially if they are still sedated.

questions.stem: Two providers give the same sedation drugs. What primarily distinguishes the CRNA's care as MAC?
options: Qualification and readiness to provide GA if needed
The depth of sedation achieved and the drugs chosen for the case
questions.explanation: MAC is defined by the provider's qualification and readiness to convert to GA, not by the drugs or depth.

questions.stem: A 4-hour MAC record has ECG, SpO2, and BP but no capnography or temperature monitoring. Which monitoring elements are missing?
options: Arterial line pressure and cerebral oximetry
questions.explanation: Continuous monitoring during MAC includes oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature when indicated; a 4-hour case indicates temperature.

questions.stem: Why does even a healthy patient need a full anesthesia preop evaluation before MAC?
options: MAC can progress to GA, so its evaluation is comparable to GA
It replaces the gastroenterologist's own H&P
A full exam is required for ASA III or higher, and a brief one for ASA I–II
The exam replaces the gastroenterologist's H&P
questions.explanation: MAC can progress to GA at any time, so the evaluation must be comparable to GA.

questions.stem: A patient under MAC becomes deeply sedated. Which statement correctly describes the service?
options: MAC is an anesthesia service, so the case remains MAC at any depth
MAC ends when the patient is deeply sedated
The case becomes moderate sedation once the patient is deeply sedated
questions.explanation: MAC is a specific anesthesia service for procedures, not a depth level.

questions.stem: Why do MAC cases require evaluation, monitoring, and provider presence standards comparable to GA?
options: Sedation can progress to general anesthesia at any time
MAC cases last longer than comparable GA cases and need more oversight
MAC patients are ASA III or higher
questions.explanation: Because sedation can slide into GA without warning, MAC requires the same evaluation, monitoring, and presence standards as GA.

questions.stem: After MAC, the handoff is verbal but PACU assessment and vitals are not documented. Which requirement is missed?
options: Surgeon approval of the planned sedation depth before discharge
questions.explanation: ASA requires postanesthesia monitoring and documentation after MAC.

questions.stem: Why might an amnestic drug be useful during MAC even if analgesia is adequate?
options: Patients may otherwise recall parts of the procedure
Amnestic agents prevent movement during stimulation
questions.explanation: Amnestic drugs reduce recall during MAC; they do not provide analgesia or immobility.

questions.stem: IV midazolam and fentanyl titrated together for moderate sedation represent what type of delivery strategy?
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation is often given intravenously and multimodally, combining an anxiolytic or sedative with an analgesic.

questions.stem: A remote IR suite lacks backup suction and capnography. What equipment standard applies?
options: Standards and equipment must match the OR
Remote sites may use reduced equipment
Capnography can be replaced by SpO2 at remote sites
Backup suction is needed in the main OR, where cases are longer
questions.explanation: MAC standards and equipment must be the same in remote locations as in the OR.

questions.stem: Which FIVE preop considerations matter most for a frail patient with COPD and kyphosis undergoing a long shoulder MAC? (Select 5)
options: Whether he can tolerate the position for the expected duration
Likelihood of airway obstruction or loss of airway access
Ability to cooperate under the drapes
The analgesic requirement for the procedure
A plan for conversion to GA
questions.explanation: The MAC preop assessment covers tolerance of position and duration, airway obstruction or loss of access, analgesic requirement, cooperation, and a conversion plan.

questions.stem: A patient with severe cardiovascular disease is scheduled for MAC. Which planning priority is most important?
options: Prepare for hemodynamic instability and conversion
Plan a lighter sedation level so instability is unlikely
Limit monitoring to SpO2 to reduce stimulation
questions.explanation: Severe cardiovascular disease is a listed risk condition. Planning for instability and conversion is essential.

questions.stem: A patient under MAC becomes unresponsive to pain. What is the correct interpretation of the service and provider responsibility?
options: It is still MAC, and the provider must manage the patient at GA depth
It is no longer MAC; it is now moderate sedation
It is no longer MAC; it requires a new consent
It is still MAC as long as the patient continues to respond to pain
questions.explanation: MAC depth may range from minimal sedation to GA; the provider must be ready to manage the airway at any depth.

questions.stem: Who meets the ASA requirement to provide MAC for a high-risk TAVR case?
options: The CRNA, as a qualified anesthesia provider
The nurse educator, if credentialed in sedation
Any of the three, depending on depth
questions.explanation: MAC must be provided by a qualified anesthesia provider.

questions.stem: Which statement about MAC versus moderate sedation is false?
options: MAC and moderate sedation are identical services
MAC is provided by an anesthesia professional
MAC can include deeper levels than moderate sedation
Moderate sedation should not intentionally render the patient unresponsive
questions.explanation: MAC and moderate sedation differ in provider, possible depth, and readiness to convert to GA.

questions.stem: Which causes most commonly lead MAC cases to convert to GA?
options: Failed block, intolerance of MAC, and hypoxia or obstruction
Aspiration, hypothermia, and loss of IV access
Surgeon request, PONV, and refractory hemodynamic instability
questions.explanation: Large series show failed neuraxial or regional anesthesia, inability to tolerate MAC, and hypoxia or airway obstruction as the most common conversion reasons.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which THREE developments during MAC should trigger consideration of conversion to GA? (Select 3)
options: Infiltrated IV with no other access
The surgeon extends the incision into the abdomen
Mild anxiety before incision that settles with reassurance
Stable vital signs with a comfortable patient
A brief BP dip that responds to one dose of ephedrine
questions.explanation: Triggers include hypercarbia, loss of IV access, procedural change, agitation, coughing, aspiration, altered mental status, refractory instability, and prolonged surgery.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Repeated coughing develops during MAC and threatens the procedure. How should this be treated conceptually?
options: Coughing is a trigger that may require conversion
Coughing resolves with more supplemental oxygen
Coughing means the block is working
Coughing should be treated with more propofol to deepen
questions.explanation: Coughing is a listed trigger for conversion because it can threaten the airway and the procedure.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient moves during a critical neural portion of surgery. When does conversion to GA become necessary?
options: When the procedure cannot continue safely under MAC
When SpO2 falls below 90% for more than 30 seconds
As soon as the patient stops responding to voice
When the case runs 30 minutes past its scheduled time
questions.explanation: Conversion is indicated when the procedure cannot safely continue under MAC. Patient movement near neural structures is one example.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: The patient becomes agitated, BIS rises, and the IV is swollen and cool during propofol MAC. What is the best next step?
options: Treat this as loss of IV access and plan conversion or a new line
Increase the propofol rate on the same line to overcome the agitation
Give a propofol bolus through the same line
Add fentanyl through the same line
questions.explanation: An infiltrated IV means no drug is reaching the patient. Loss of IV access is a conversion trigger; more drug through the same line will not help and can cause tissue injury.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A stable MAC tempts the anesthesia provider to work on the next chart. Which safety principle is at risk?
options: Continuous vigilance and readiness for airway control
Reducing monitoring for stable patients to limit alarm fatigue
questions.explanation: MAC requires continuous vigilance and readiness for airway control, even when the case seems stable.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Before MAC, what expectation should be set regarding wakefulness and recall?
options: They may remain awake and remember parts of the procedure
They will be fully asleep with no recall
They will feel no discomfort at all
They will not need monitoring once they are comfortable
questions.explanation: Patients should know they may be awake and remember parts of the procedure; promising full sleep sets up awareness complaints.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient later complains, "I was supposed to be asleep." Which preoperative step would most likely have prevented this mismatch?
options: Explaining MAC and that GA remains possible if needed
Removing airway equipment to calm the patient
Giving a larger midazolam dose before entering the OR
Giving prophylactic ondansetron before the start of the case
questions.explanation: Mismatch between the planned anesthetic and patient expectations contributes to complaints of awareness. Setting expectations, including possible conversion, prevents this.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Why should patients be warned that sore throat is possible even when MAC is planned?
options: If the case converts to GA, an airway device may be placed
The nasal cannula irritates and dries the throat during long cases
The capnography line passes into the throat
questions.explanation: Conversion to GA may require an LMA or ETT, which can cause a sore throat; setting this expectation prevents complaints.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which TWO expectations should be discussed before MAC? (Select 2)
options: They will be fully asleep for the entire case
They will be fully asleep throughout
They will be discharged directly from the OR
questions.explanation: Patients should know they may feel brief discomfort, may need to follow instructions, may remember parts, and may be converted to GA if needed.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC for orthopedic surgery, the patient may intermittently hear saws and conversation. How should this be framed beforehand?
options: Patients may hear sounds and wake intermittently
The patient will be fully asleep throughout
Hearing sounds means the block failed
questions.explanation: Patients under MAC may hear procedural sounds and wake intermittently; setting this expectation reduces distress.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A MAC patient obstructs and SpO2 falls to 84%. What is the first priority?
options: Relieve the obstruction and support ventilation
Increase the propofol to prevent movement
Increase oxygen flow to 10 L/min by face mask
Ask the proceduralist to finish quickly
questions.explanation: Airway obstruction is treated first by relieving it (jaw thrust, airway adjunct) and supporting ventilation.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient becomes agitated and moves during a critical part of MAC. What is the best next step?
options: Assess causes and prepare to convert if unsafe
Give a large propofol bolus immediately
Give a propofol bolus to hold still for the critical step
Ask the patient to hold still and continue
questions.explanation: Agitation is a trigger. Look for causes like hypoxia or pain and convert if the procedure cannot continue safely.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During airway rescue, the video laryngoscope is dead and no induction drug is prepared. Which planning principle was violated?
options: The conversion plan must be in place before the procedure starts
Conversion plans are needed for planned deep sedation cases
Conversion plans are needed for ASA IV patients having MAC
Conversion plans are made once problems arise
questions.explanation: A conversion-to-GA plan, including equipment and drugs, must be ready before starting MAC.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Vomiting with suspected aspiration occurs during EGD under MAC. What type of conversion trigger is this?
questions.explanation: Aspiration is listed as a trigger for conversion because it threatens the airway.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Three MAC patients differ: one has persistent ETCO2 65 despite stimulation and jaw thrust; the others have mild anxiety or a small HR rise. Which patient has a true conversion trigger?
options: Patient A, with hypercarbia despite support
Patient C, with a small HR increase
None of them meets a conversion trigger at this point in the case
questions.explanation: Persistent hypercarbia despite airway support is a conversion trigger. Mild anxiety and small HR changes are expected and managed within MAC.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A diagnostic laparoscopy unexpectedly becomes an open exploration. Why does this procedural change favor conversion to GA?
options: The planned sedation no longer matches the procedure
It lowers infection risk by shortening the procedure
questions.explanation: When the procedure changes, the original sedation plan may no longer be safe or adequate.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: After additional midazolam, a MAC patient becomes more restless and combative. What is the best explanation?
options: Deeper sedation can cause disinhibition rather than calm
She needs more midazolam to reach adequate depth
She has had an inadequate block that needs more sedation
questions.explanation: Oversedation can cause disinhibition and restlessness; adding more drug risks airway compromise.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which THREE causes most commonly lead MAC cases to convert to GA? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Failed blocks, intolerance of MAC, and hypoxia or obstruction are the most common reasons for conversion.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A spinal anesthetic fails during hip surgery under MAC and the patient becomes uncomfortable. What is the best next step?
options: Increase sedation until the patient stops moving
Add propofol boluses until the patient stops moving
Give midazolam for anxiety and continue under MAC
questions.explanation: Failed neuraxial anesthesia is a common reason for conversion. Adding sedation alone may lead to unsafe depth.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient was promised complete sleep during MAC but later recalls the procedure. What complication is most likely to be reported?
questions.explanation: Mismatched expectations about MAC can lead to complaints of awareness.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Two similar MAC patients receive different preop counseling. Which patient is more likely to report dissatisfaction from awareness?
options: The second patient is more likely to report awareness and dissatisfaction
The first patient is more likely to complain, since she was told she may remember
The second patient is less likely to remember because expectations alter amnesia
questions.explanation: Clear communication about MAC sets realistic expectations; mismatched expectations lead to awareness complaints.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, the patient becomes confused, combative, and unable to follow commands. Which conversion trigger applies?
questions.explanation: Altered mental status that prevents safe continuation is a conversion trigger.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Severe hypotension and bradycardia persist despite initial treatment during MAC. What should be considered next?
options: Increase the propofol infusion to blunt the stress response
Increase sedation to reduce the patient's stress response
questions.explanation: Hemodynamic instability is a trigger for conversion if it prevents safe continuation.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Why should patients be told they may need to follow commands during MAC?
questions.explanation: Many MAC procedures require patient cooperation, so patients should expect to follow instructions.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During a quiet MAC, the anesthesia provider focuses on another patient's chart and waits for alarms to redirect attention. Which principle is violated?
options: Continuous vigilance with immediate airway readiness
Vigilance concentrated at induction and emergence
Vigilance when alarms sound or the surgeon asks
Vigilance focused on the proceduralist's needs
questions.explanation: MAC demands continuous vigilance and immediate readiness for airway control, the same as GA.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which preoperative statement reveals unrealistic expectations about MAC and requires clarification?
options: "I'll be completely asleep and won't remember anything."
"I might hear some noises, and that's fine."
"I may feel some pressure but not sharp pain."
"You'll be watching my breathing the whole time."
questions.explanation: Expecting complete sleep and no memory conflicts with MAC and predicts awareness complaints.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: When MAC must convert to GA, which resource must already be immediately available?
questions.explanation: Immediate availability of airway adjuncts and advanced airway equipment is required in the MAC environment.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which event during MAC is NOT by itself a conversion trigger?
options: Mild preprocedure anxiety that settles with reassurance
Persistent coughing that prevents the surgeon from working
Hypotension that does not respond to treatment
questions.explanation: Mild anxiety is expected and managed with reassurance and anxiolysis. Coughing, aspiration, and refractory instability are conversion triggers.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A restless patient repeatedly reaches toward the field late in a MAC. What is the best response before giving more sedative?
options: Reassess the cause and convert to GA if MAC is unsafe
Keep adding small boluses until the patient is still
Give larger sedative boluses until the patient stops moving
Give an opioid bolus and continue as planned
questions.explanation: Restlessness may reflect pain, position, or a full bladder, and more drug risks deeper-than-intended sedation. Reassess and be ready to convert.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient asks whether memory is guaranteed to be absent during propofol MAC. What is the most accurate answer?
options: You may remember parts of the procedure
You will remember nothing at all
You will be fully awake and remember everything
questions.explanation: Recall under MAC depends on depth and drugs; patients may remember parts of the procedure.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A planned 1-hour MAC has extended to 3 hours, and the patient is restless, requiring more propofol and beginning to obstruct. Which conversion trigger is present?
options: Prolonged surgery; consider conversion to GA
Loss of IV access; place a new IV
questions.explanation: Prolonged surgery increases restlessness and oversedation risk and is a conversion trigger.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, RR is 6 and ETCO2 62 despite repeated stimulation while SpO2 remains acceptable on oxygen. What does this mean for the plan?
options: Persistent hypercarbia is a trigger to consider conversion
It is normal under deep sedation
It is acceptable while SpO2 stays above 90% on supplemental oxygen
questions.explanation: Persistent hypoventilation despite stimulation signals inadequate ventilation and is a conversion trigger.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A procedure unexpectedly becomes much more invasive while MAC is underway. What should be done?
options: Reassess and consider conversion to GA
Increase oxygen and continue with the current plan
questions.explanation: Procedural change is a trigger for conversion because the plan may no longer be appropriate.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which FOUR expectations should be discussed before MAC? (Select 4)
options: She may remember parts of the procedure
Conversion to general anesthesia is possible
She may hear conversations in the room
She will not need an airway device under any circumstances
questions.explanation: Patients should know they may be awake, remember, hear conversations, and be converted to GA if needed.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which drug is most commonly used as the primary hypnotic for moderate-to-deep MAC sedation?
questions.explanation: Propofol is the most common MAC drug because of its rapid onset and offset and easy titration.

questions.stem: Which receptor mechanism produces propofol's hypnotic effect?
questions.explanation: Propofol potentiates GABA-A receptor activity, producing hypnosis and amnesia. NMDA antagonism is ketamine and alpha-2 agonism is dexmedetomidine.

questions.stem: Why can an elderly patient with poor cardiac reserve become profoundly hypotensive after a propofol dose tolerated by a younger healthy adult?
options: Propofol's effect depends on age, cardiac reserve, and volume status
Propofol causes more pain on injection in the elderly
Propofol has active metabolites that accumulate in heart failure
Older patients have a smaller volume of distribution only
questions.explanation: The slide states clinical effect is strongly influenced by age, cardiac reserve, volume status, and co-administered drugs.

questions.stem: A deeply sedated patient still withdraws and moans at incision while receiving propofol alone. What important drug property explains this?
options: The propofol dose was too low for sedation
The patient has developed tolerance to propofol
questions.explanation: Propofol is a hypnotic without analgesic properties, so painful stimulation still causes a response.

questions.stem: Which FOUR strategies reduce propofol injection pain? (Select 4)
options: Pretreat with lidocaine and venous occlusion
Inject into a fast-running IV line
Inject rapidly into the hand vein
questions.explanation: Larger veins, slower injection, a fast-running line, lidocaine with venous occlusion, and opioid pretreatment reduce propofol injection pain.

questions.stem: Propofol burns through a small hand IV. What is the best immediate technique change?
options: Slow the injection and give it into a fast-flowing carrier
Push faster to shorten the exposure time
Move to a smaller vein distal to the IV
Mix the propofol with an equal volume of saline first
questions.explanation: Slower injection into a fast-running line reduces pain. A larger antecubital vein or lidocaine pretreatment would also help.

questions.stem: Which pharmacokinetic property makes propofol useful for both brief sedation and prolonged TIVA?
options: Rapid onset with rapid redistribution, allowing easy titration
Long duration of action that suits lengthy procedures without redosing
Strong analgesia that reduces opioid needs
questions.explanation: Propofol's fast onset and redistribution make it easy to titrate across very different depths and durations.

questions.stem: Which THREE adverse effects should be anticipated after a large propofol bolus? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Propofol causes respiratory depression, apnea, hypotension, and injection pain. Emergence reactions and hypersalivation are ketamine effects; chest wall rigidity is an opioid effect.

questions.stem: A patient receiving propofol no longer responds to voice. What change in risk should be recognized immediately?
options: Sedation may now carry the risks of GA with an open airway
The patient is at ideal moderate sedation for EGD
The patient has dropped to minimal sedation depth
The patient needs flumazenil to restore responsiveness
questions.explanation: Loss of verbal responsiveness should prompt recognition that sedation may be approaching GA with an unprotected airway.

questions.stem: Why is a second IV reasonable during prolonged deep propofol sedation?
options: Deep propofol cases depend on reliable IV delivery
Propofol requires two IVs for dilution of the emulsion
A second IV is required for blood draws
A second IV prevents injection pain
questions.explanation: Deep propofol cases depend on reliable IV access; losing the only IV can lead to awareness or delay rescue drugs.

questions.stem: A sedative causes delayed onset followed by perineal tingling and pruritus. Which agent is most likely?
options: Fospropofol, a water-soluble prodrug converted to propofol
Propofol, a lipid emulsion that causes burning in small veins
questions.explanation: Fospropofol is a water-soluble prodrug; conversion to propofol delays onset, and perineal paresthesia and pruritus are typical side effects.

questions.stem: Compared with propofol, what onset-and-recovery pattern should be expected with fospropofol?
options: The fospropofol patient takes longer to fall asleep and to wake up
The fospropofol patient falls asleep faster
Both have identical onset and recovery
The propofol patient takes longer to wake up because of redistribution
questions.explanation: Fospropofol must be converted to propofol, so onset is delayed and recovery is slower.

questions.stem: Perineal paresthesia and generalized itching occur after an IV sedative without rash. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Perineal paresthesia and pruritus are characteristic of fospropofol.

questions.stem: What is the current U.S. status of fospropofol according to the lecture?
options: It is not currently approved for use in the United States
It is approved in the US for both GA and MAC sedation
It is approved in the US for MAC but not GA
It is approved in the US for ICU sedation
questions.explanation: Fospropofol is not currently approved for use in the US, and it is not approved for GA.

questions.stem: For which clinical use was fospropofol originally developed?
questions.explanation: Fospropofol was developed for MAC sedation; it is not approved for GA.

questions.stem: Why would fospropofol be expected to cause less injection pain than propofol?
options: Less injection pain, since fospropofol is water-soluble
More injection pain, since fospropofol is more concentrated
The same injection pain, since both become propofol
Injection pain that occurs mainly in children and small veins
questions.explanation: Fospropofol is water-soluble rather than a lipid emulsion, so it causes less injection pain.

questions.stem: A fospropofol sedation protocol proposes pulse oximetry alone and no airway cart. What is the major safety flaw?
options: Providers must be ready to rescue from deep sedation or GA
Nothing, since fospropofol lacks respiratory depression
Pulse oximetry alone is enough for this drug
Airway equipment is unnecessary for prodrugs
questions.explanation: Fospropofol can still cause respiratory depression and hypotension, so rescue capability and appropriate monitoring are required.

questions.stem: Which sedative best fits a short outpatient procedure requiring rapid onset and rapid recovery?
questions.explanation: Propofol has rapid onset and recovery. Fospropofol and dexmedetomidine have slower onset, and midazolam can prolong recovery.

questions.stem: Why can chronic benzodiazepine exposure make propofol response less predictable?
options: Co-administered or chronic sedative exposure alters effect
Benzodiazepines block propofol metabolism in the liver
Propofol is antagonized by GABA agonists
questions.explanation: The slide notes propofol's effect is influenced by co-administered drugs. Chronic sedative exposure is also on the caution list.

questions.stem: Propofol alone produces hypnosis and amnesia, but the patient still reacts to incision. Which component is missing?
options: It provides hypnosis and amnesia; analgesia is missing
It provides analgesia; amnesia is missing
It provides analgesia and amnesia; hypnosis is missing
It provides dissociation; amnesia is missing
questions.explanation: Propofol provides hypnosis and amnesia without analgesia, so painful stimuli still cause responses.

questions.stem: A hypovolemic patient with active GI bleeding receives propofol. Which hemodynamic effect is most likely exaggerated?
questions.explanation: Propofol causes vasodilation and myocardial depression, which are exaggerated in hypovolemic patients.

questions.stem: Which strategy best reduces propofol injection pain when only small peripheral veins are available?
options: Opioid pretreatment, lidocaine with venous occlusion, and a fast-running carrier
Rapid injection into a small vein
Chilling the propofol, then injecting quickly to shorten the exposure time
questions.explanation: Opioid pretreatment, lidocaine with venous occlusion, larger veins, slower injection, and a fast-running carrier all reduce propofol injection pain.

questions.stem: An 80-kg patient receives propofol 100 mcg/kg/min from a 10 mg/mL solution. What pump rate is required?
questions.explanation: 100 mcg/kg/min × 80 kg = 8,000 mcg/min = 8 mg/min = 480 mg/hr. At 10 mg/mL, that is 48 mL/hr.

questions.stem: Why is loss of verbal responsiveness during propofol sedation a critical warning point?
options: Propofol can quickly deepen to GA with loss of airway reflexes
Propofol stops working at this point
Propofol causes seizures when verbal response is lost
Propofol causes hypertension and tachycardia once verbal response is lost
questions.explanation: Propofol can rapidly move a patient from deep sedation to GA with loss of airway reflexes.

questions.stem: Which common sedation drug provides hypnosis without analgesia?
questions.explanation: Propofol provides no analgesia; ketamine and the opioids do.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient needs propofol 50 mcg/kg/min from a 10 mg/mL solution. What pump rate is required?
questions.explanation: 50 × 70 = 3,500 mcg/min = 3.5 mg/min = 210 mg/hr. At 10 mg/mL, that is 21 mL/hr.

questions.stem: Which sedative is especially useful when preserving spontaneous ventilation is a priority in severe OSA?
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine provides sedation and anxiolysis with minimal respiratory depression, which makes it attractive for OSA and awake intubation.

questions.stem: For MRI sedation in severe OSA, which drug profile best balances sedation with preservation of ventilation?
options: Dexmedetomidine with slower onset and bradycardia risk
Propofol with rapid onset and apnea risk
Remifentanil with rapid titration and respiratory depression
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine has minimal respiratory depression but slower onset and risk of bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.stem: A dexmedetomidine load is followed by marked bradycardia and hypotension. How should this be interpreted?
options: An emergence reaction from dissociative effects
questions.explanation: Bradycardia and hypotension are the key considerations with dexmedetomidine, along with slower onset.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient needs dexmedetomidine 1 mcg/kg over 10 minutes from a 4 mcg/mL solution. What pump rate delivers the load?
questions.explanation: The load is 70 mcg, or 17.5 mL at 4 mcg/mL. Delivering 17.5 mL over 10 minutes requires 105 mL/hr.

questions.stem: A frail 82-year-old with cirrhosis needs brief sedation and rapid recovery. Which benzodiazepine best fits?
options: Midazolam, since it is short-acting and well tolerated in older adults
questions.explanation: Remimazolam's esterase metabolism gives a short, predictable offset even with hepatic disease. Midazolam can accumulate in cirrhosis and older patients.

questions.stem: How should recovery after remimazolam differ in severe hepatic or renal failure compared with a healthy patient?
options: Similar in both, since tissue esterases metabolize it
Prolonged in A, since it is cleared by the liver
Prolonged in B, since it is cleared by the kidneys
Prolonged in both, since it depends on both organs
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is metabolized by tissue esterases, independent of liver and kidney function.

questions.stem: After remimazolam and fentanyl, a patient is somnolent and hypoventilating. Which antagonist reverses the benzodiazepine component?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is a benzodiazepine and is reversed by flumazenil; naloxone reverses the fentanyl component.

questions.stem: Which sedative best matches organ-independent esterase metabolism in combined hepatic and renal dysfunction?
questions.explanation: The note says esterase metabolism makes remimazolam good for liver/kidney problems and OSA patients.

questions.stem: A frail patient with severe aortic stenosis needs short sedation with minimal hemodynamic disturbance and predictable recovery. Which drug best fits?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam offers hemodynamic stability and predictable recovery from esterase metabolism. Hypotension and respiratory depression remain possible, so titrate carefully.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about remimazolam are correct? (Select 2)
options: It has a long context-sensitive half-time
questions.explanation: Remimazolam enhances GABA-A activity and is reversed by flumazenil. Esterase metabolism gives a short offset; it provides no analgesia and can depress breathing.

questions.stem: Compared with remimazolam, why is midazolam more likely to prolong recovery in an older patient?
options: The midazolam patient, since midazolam can prolong recovery
The remimazolam patient, since it accumulates in older adults
Both equally, since both are benzodiazepines
questions.explanation: Midazolam can prolong recovery, especially in older patients; remimazolam has a short, predictable offset.

questions.stem: Why is the combination of midazolam and fentanyl particularly risky for ventilation?
questions.explanation: Midazolam causes respiratory depression, especially with opioids. Sedatives and opioids have synergistic respiratory depression.

questions.stem: A hypotensive patient requires painful burn dressing care while preserving spontaneous ventilation. Which drug best fits?
questions.explanation: Ketamine provides dissociative sedation and analgesia, supports BP, and usually preserves ventilation.

questions.stem: Which THREE effects should be anticipated after subanesthetic ketamine? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Ketamine considerations include emergence reactions, hypersalivation, hypertension, and possible airway complications.

questions.stem: A child breathes spontaneously after ketamine. Why should capnography and airway rescue equipment still remain in use?
options: Airway complications remain possible; keep monitoring
Ketamine's preserved reflexes make capnography optional
Ketamine sedation does not require capnography or airway equipment
questions.explanation: Ketamine preserves ventilation more often than propofol, but laryngospasm and other airway complications can still occur.

questions.stem: Why can a ketamine-propofol combination be advantageous for a brief painful procedure?
options: Ketamine adds analgesia and offsets propofol's hypotension
The mix extends recovery so patients are more comfortable afterward
questions.explanation: Ketofol combines ketamine's analgesia and sympathetic support with propofol's hypnosis, balancing their side effects.

questions.stem: Which drug best provides rapidly titratable, short-lived analgesia for a brief painful stimulus, and what is its major tradeoff?
options: Morphine, with a long duration that outlasts the procedure
Dexmedetomidine, with analgesia but no hypnosis
questions.explanation: Remifentanil is highly titratable and short-acting but causes significant respiratory depression.

questions.stem: After a rapid high-dose fentanyl bolus, ventilation becomes impossible because the chest is rigid. What complication occurred?
questions.explanation: Rapid or high-dose fentanyl can cause chest wall rigidity, treated with neuromuscular blockade.

questions.stem: During remifentanil MAC, RR falls to 6 and ETCO2 rises. What is the best immediate response?
options: Continue, since remifentanil will wear off in minutes
questions.explanation: Remifentanil causes significant respiratory depression. Reduce the infusion and support ventilation.

questions.stem: Which common sedative adjunct provides rapid-onset analgesia rather than hypnosis?
questions.explanation: Fentanyl provides rapid-onset analgesia and is useful for painful procedures.

questions.stem: Which FOUR drugs provide clinically useful analgesia during sedation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Opioids and ketamine provide analgesia. Propofol and benzodiazepines do not.

questions.stem: A patient has a strong history of unpleasant emergence reactions. Which sedative would be least attractive?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is associated with emergence reactions.

questions.stem: During carotid angiography, HR falls to 42 after starting sedation. Which agent is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine commonly causes bradycardia and hypotension. Ketamine tends to raise HR and BP.

questions.stem: A patient receives midazolam plus fentanyl. Which drug provides the analgesic component?
options: Fentanyl, since midazolam has no analgesic effect
Midazolam, since it has strong analgesic effects
Both equally, since both are sedatives
questions.explanation: Fentanyl provides analgesia; midazolam provides anxiolysis, sedation, and amnesia.

questions.stem: Severe liver disease is present, but rapid titration, amnesia, and quick recovery are needed. Which benzodiazepine best fits?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam provides rapid, titratable sedation and amnesia with organ-independent esterase metabolism.

questions.stem: Which of these sedatives can be reversed with flumazenil?
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is a benzodiazepine and is reversible with flumazenil; the others have no flumazenil effect.

questions.stem: A dexmedetomidine load is started shortly before the procedure, but the patient remains awake after 5 minutes. What best explains this?
options: Dexmedetomidine has a slower onset than many sedatives
Dexmedetomidine needs an opioid to produce sedation
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine has a slower onset, so loading should start earlier.

questions.stem: Which sedative best preserves ventilation when rapid onset is not essential?
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine has minimal respiratory depression but slower onset.

questions.stem: Copious secretions develop after ketamine. Which adverse effect is responsible?
questions.explanation: Hypersalivation is a listed ketamine adverse effect.

questions.stem: Which sedative-analgesic produces dissociation primarily through NMDA antagonism?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is an NMDA antagonist that provides sedation, analgesia, and dissociative anesthesia.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient needs remifentanil 0.1 mcg/kg/min from a 50 mcg/mL solution. What pump rate is required?
questions.explanation: 0.1 × 70 = 7 mcg/min = 420 mcg/hr. At 50 mcg/mL, that is 8.4 mL/hr.

questions.stem: Which sedative should generally be avoided or used very cautiously in severe baseline bradycardia?
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine can cause bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.stem: Which THREE effects are expected from midazolam used for procedural sedation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Midazolam provides anxiolysis, sedation, and amnesia but no analgesia.

questions.stem: Small doses of midazolam and fentanyl together cause apnea. What pharmacologic interaction explains this?
options: Sedatives and opioids have synergistic respiratory depression
Fentanyl caused chest wall rigidity that prevented breathing
questions.explanation: Sedatives and opioids depress breathing synergistically, so small doses together can cause apnea.

questions.stem: Propofol and remifentanil are combined for sedation. Which adverse-effect pairing should be anticipated?
questions.explanation: Propofol causes apnea and hypotension; remifentanil causes significant respiratory depression. Together, apnea is likely.

questions.stem: Electrocautery is used near the face while oxygen flows beneath drapes. Which complication is most specifically increased?
options: Surgical fire from an oxygen-enriched environment
Postoperative visual loss from head position and pressure
questions.explanation: Fire risk rises when oxygen pools near an ignition source in head and neck procedures. Reduce FiO2 to the lowest safe level and let oxygen disperse before cautery.

questions.stem: During facial MAC with open oxygen, what visible draping feature most increases fire risk?
options: Drapes tented near the face where oxygen can collect
The pulse oximeter on the finger
The BP cuff cycling on the arm closest to the field
questions.explanation: Tented drapes trap oxygen near the face, creating an oxygen-enriched environment where cautery can ignite a fire.

questions.stem: During head-and-neck MAC with electrocautery, what oxygen-delivery principle best reduces fire risk?
questions.explanation: Tinnitus and metallic taste are early LAST signs. Your note flags "lots of lidocaine IV + local → LAST." Doses from every source add together.

questions.stem: A patient suddenly coughs and moves during electrocautery near the face. What immediate safety concern becomes dominant?
options: Laryngospasm from airway stimulation at a light plane
Bronchospasm from deep TIVA with a secured airway in place
Local anesthetic toxicity from a forearm block
questions.explanation: Gagging at a light plane with secretions or a scope near the larynx can trigger laryngospasm, which may need positive pressure or airway instrumentation.

questions.stem: During MAC, the patient regurgitates and desaturates. What should be the first priority?
options: Stop stimulation, jaw thrust, positive pressure with 100% O2
Raise nasal cannula flow to 6 L/min and observe
Give flumazenil to reverse benzodiazepine effect
Give glycopyrrolate and wait for the spasm to break
questions.explanation: Stridor progressing to silence suggests laryngospasm moving to complete closure. Stop stimulation, open the airway, and give CPAP/positive pressure; deepen or paralyze if it persists.

questions.stem: Which THREE findings should raise immediate concern for aspiration during MAC? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: MAC complications include respiratory depression and obstruction, aspiration, laryngospasm, cardiovascular instability, LAST with local or regional techniques, and fire in head and neck cases.

questions.stem: During MAC, ETCO2 rises and the patient becomes progressively somnolent despite normal SpO2 on oxygen. What complication is developing?
options: Protective reflexes were impaired without a secured airway
Sedatives raise gastric acid production and volume
NPO rules do not apply to MAC patients
Supplemental oxygen through the cannula triggered the vomiting
questions.explanation: Sedation depresses protective reflexes while leaving the airway unprotected. NORA closed claims show aspiration nearly twice as often.

questions.stem: A deeply sedated patient becomes hypotensive after repeated propofol boluses. What mechanism is most likely?
options: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity from the block
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular instability from anesthetic drugs or underlying disease is a listed complication. Dexmedetomidine causes bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.stem: During sedation, a patient becomes apneic immediately after an opioid bolus. Which complication should be considered first?
options: Use the lowest O2 needed and avoid oxygen pooling under drapes
Increase O2 flow to prevent desaturation
Switch from nasal cannula to a face mask at 10 L/min before cautery
Cover the face fully with drapes
questions.explanation: Fire risk comes from oxygen enrichment near ignition sources. Minimizing O2 and venting the drapes lowers risk; a secured airway may be safer if high O2 is needed.

questions.stem: A patient under MAC develops upper-airway obstruction with snoring and falling tidal volumes. What is the best first maneuver?
options: Hypercarbia from the nasal cannula oxygen
questions.explanation: Agitation followed by seizure after regional anesthesia is classic LAST. It is listed when MAC accompanies regional techniques.

questions.stem: Jaw thrust fails to relieve obstruction and SpO2 continues to fall. What is the next priority?
options: Continued nasal oxygen while waiting it out
Observation, since laryngospasm resolves under MAC
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm during MAC can require positive-pressure ventilation or airway instrumentation, sometimes with a muscle relaxant.

questions.stem: A patient vomits during MAC but remains spontaneously breathing. What airway-protection concern should dominate management?
options: Fire: oxygen-enriched environment during head and neck cases
LAST: propofol infusion given without local anesthetic
Laryngospasm: deep sedation with a secured airway
Fire: dry drapes in a room-air environment without cautery
questions.explanation: Fire risk comes from oxygen enrichment near cautery in head and neck cases. LAST requires local anesthetic, and laryngospasm comes from airway stimulation at light planes.

questions.stem: During MAC in a remote location, severe hypotension develops and no vasopressors are immediately available. Which systems failure is exposed?
questions.explanation: Rising CO2 and somnolence show respiratory depression. Hypercarbia is also a trigger for conversion.

questions.stem: A patient becomes profoundly bradycardic after dexmedetomidine. What should the provider do first?
options: Track the total local anesthetic dose from all sources
Give extra propofol to prevent seizures
Use higher concentrations with smaller volumes to cut the dose
questions.explanation: LAST risk comes from cumulative dose. IV lidocaine, blocks, and surgical infiltration all count toward the maximum.

questions.stem: During ketamine sedation, laryngospasm develops despite preserved spontaneous breathing beforehand. What does this illustrate?
options: Topical lidocaine applied to the vocal cords
A secured airway with deep GA
Local anesthesia of a distal extremity
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is triggered by airway stimulation at light planes, such as secretions near the cords. Topical anesthesia of the cords blunts the reflex rather than triggering it.

questions.stem: After a sedative bolus, the patient becomes unresponsive, apneic, and hypotensive. Which overall transition has most likely occurred?
options: Remote sites limit access to help and airway resources
NORA procedures last longer than comparable OR cases
questions.explanation: NORA locations are remote, with limited help and airway resources, so respiratory events can become catastrophic.

questions.stem: A patient under MAC repeatedly obstructs because the procedural position limits airway access. What should be considered before giving more sedative?
options: Hypothermia from cold irrigation fluids in the GI suite
questions.explanation: Capnography detects hypoventilation and apnea early, preventing unrecognized respiratory depression.

questions.stem: In a high-fire-risk facial procedure, why is oxygen concentration more important than total flow alone?
options: Airway obstruction from jaw position and tongue fall
questions.explanation: Aspiration can cause bronchospasm and hypoxemia. EGD increases aspiration risk under sedation.

questions.stem: A remote-procedure team lacks a clear plan for who will stop the procedure during an airway emergency. Which safety principle is missing?
options: Cardiovascular instability from drugs or procedure
Respiratory depression with hypercarbia from sedation
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular instability is a listed complication. Vagal responses or drug effects can cause hypotension and bradycardia.

questions.stem: Why is it incorrect to think MAC safety is only about ventilation?
options: Respiratory problems lead, but other complications need planning
Respiratory problems are the meaningful MAC risk
Complications arise mainly at the moment of conversion to GA
Fire and LAST outnumber respiratory events in MAC claims
questions.explanation: Respiratory depression and obstruction are central, but aspiration, laryngospasm, cardiovascular instability, LAST, and fire also need planning.

questions.stem: A MAC patient develops partial obstruction with snoring. What is the best first intervention?
options: Jaw thrust or reposition the airway
Increase sedation to relax the airway
Give IV lidocaine to relax the airway
questions.explanation: Partial obstruction often responds to airway maneuvers. Increasing sedation worsens obstruction.

questions.stem: After propofol, the capnogram disappears and airway maneuvers fail. What is the next step?
options: Bag-mask ventilate and prepare for airway instrumentation
Wait briefly for propofol to redistribute and breathing
Give flumazenil and continue jaw thrust
Increase nasal cannula flow and reassess
questions.explanation: If airway maneuvers fail, provide positive-pressure ventilation and be ready for advanced airway management.

questions.stem: A patient with severe cardiomyopathy becomes hypotensive during propofol MAC. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Anesthetic drug effects combined with underlying heart disease
Supine positioning compressing the vena cava in an obese patient
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular instability during MAC comes from anesthetic drugs or the patient's underlying disease.

questions.stem: Which complication is especially associated with head-and-neck MAC using open oxygen and cautery?
questions.explanation: Fire risk is highest in oxygen-enriched head and neck procedures with cautery.

questions.stem: A patient receives IV lidocaine plus a large field block. Which complication risk increases?
options: Propofol infusion syndrome from the sedation
questions.explanation: IV lidocaine plus local infiltration raises cumulative dose and LAST risk.

questions.stem: Which anesthetic technique qualifies as true TIVA?
options: Propofol and remifentanil with no inhaled agent
All three, since each includes at least one IV drug during the case
questions.explanation: TIVA is GA delivered only with IV agents, without any inhaled anesthetic.

questions.stem: Which THREE factors favor TIVA for a patient with MH susceptibility, severe PONV history, and planned neuromonitoring? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: TIVA reduces PONV, avoids MH triggers, and supports neuromonitoring. It lacks end-tidal agent measurement and depends on IV access.

questions.stem: What key monitoring disadvantage distinguishes TIVA from volatile anesthesia?
options: No end-tidal anesthetic concentration to confirm delivery
No capnography is possible during TIVA with an airway
questions.explanation: Volatile anesthesia has end-tidal agent monitoring; TIVA has no equivalent, so line checks and processed EEG matter.

questions.stem: Why is processed EEG particularly useful when a TIVA patient is fully paralyzed?
options: It replaces the need for ASA monitors
It measures the depth of neuromuscular blockade
questions.explanation: With neuromuscular blockade, movement is unavailable as a sign of light anesthesia. Processed EEG helps assess hypnotic depth.

questions.stem: Which drug combination is most commonly used for propofol-based TIVA?
options: Propofol for hypnosis with remifentanil for analgesia
Midazolam for hypnosis with ketamine for analgesia
questions.explanation: Propofol with remifentanil or another opioid is the common TIVA combination.

questions.stem: Why must postoperative analgesia be established before stopping propofol-remifentanil TIVA?
options: Both drugs leave little residual analgesia
Propofol causes hyperalgesia that blocks later opioids
questions.explanation: Remifentanil wears off within minutes and propofol has no analgesia, so a longer-acting analgesic must be given before emergence.

questions.stem: The propofol pump alarms for occlusion, BIS rises, and HR increases. What is the most likely cause?
options: Interrupted propofol delivery causing light anesthesia
Hypercarbia from ventilator settings after positioning
questions.explanation: Pumps must be checked for disconnection, occlusion, or infiltration. Loss of delivery causes lightening and awareness risk.

questions.stem: What IV setup best reduces delivery failure during prone TIVA with tucked arms?
options: A dedicated, visible line with minimal dead space
A shared carrier line running blood products
A long extension set routed under the drapes
A hand IV tucked out of sight under the drapes
questions.explanation: A dedicated, visible line with minimal dead space ensures reliable delivery. Infiltration or disconnection under the drapes can cause awareness.

questions.stem: BIS rises despite a pump that appears to be running normally. What should be checked first?
options: The line for disconnection, occlusion, or infiltration
Nothing yet, since the pump shows no occlusion alarm
questions.explanation: Pumps can run normally while drug never reaches the patient. Check the line for disconnection, occlusion, or infiltration first.

questions.stem: During TIVA, surgical stimulation increases sharply. How should the infusions be adjusted?
options: Titrate to hemodynamics, stimulation, and signs of depth
Increase only the remifentanil and leave propofol fixed
Adjust to the BIS value alone
Adjust to heart rate changes alone
questions.explanation: TIVA infusions are titrated to patient characteristics, hemodynamics, surgical intensity, and signs of depth, not fixed doses.

questions.stem: SSEP amplitude falls markedly while MEPs remain unchanged. Which pathway is most likely affected?
options: Both sensory and motor pathways equally
questions.explanation: SSEPs monitor sensory pathways; MEPs monitor motor pathways.

questions.stem: MEPs disappear after rocuronium and increased sevoflurane. What best explains the signal loss?
options: MEPs assess motor pathways and are sensitive to volatiles and NMB
MEPs assess sensory pathways and are unaffected by drugs
MEPs are affected by opioids and remifentanil but not by volatile agents
questions.explanation: MEPs assess motor pathways and are suppressed by volatile agents and neuromuscular blockade.

questions.stem: How do volatile agents typically affect SSEP amplitude and latency?
options: No change in amplitude or latency
Latency decreases with no amplitude change
questions.explanation: Volatile agents depress SSEPs by decreasing amplitude and increasing latency.

questions.stem: If a volatile must briefly supplement TIVA during MEP monitoring, approximately what concentration may still preserve signals?
questions.explanation: Low volatile concentrations, about 0.25 MAC, may be used if MEP signals stay adequate. Higher concentrations depress MEPs.

questions.stem: The surgeon requests deeper paralysis during MEP monitoring. What is the best response?
options: Avoid or carefully titrate NMB after intubation
Give full-dose paralysis to aid surgery
Switch to volatile anesthesia to relax muscles
Stop MEP monitoring to allow paralysis
questions.explanation: NMB should be avoided or carefully titrated after intubation when muscle-recorded MEPs are monitored.

questions.stem: SSEPs deteriorate immediately after a rapid anesthetic concentration change. What should be considered before assuming neurologic injury?
options: Abrupt anesthetic changes can mimic neurologic injury
The patient definitely has spinal cord injury
The monitoring equipment is broken and needs replacing
questions.explanation: The clinical pearl says abrupt changes in anesthetic concentration can alter SSEP/MEP signals and mimic neurologic injury.

questions.stem: Which FOUR factors should be kept stable when neuromonitoring signals deteriorate? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Stable BP, hemoglobin, oxygenation, temperature, and consistent depth all support reliable evoked potentials.

questions.stem: Why is propofol-opioid TIVA preferred over volatile anesthesia when both SSEPs and MEPs are needed?
options: It minimizes anesthetic interference with evoked potentials
It provides better analgesia than volatile anesthesia does
questions.explanation: Propofol-opioid TIVA interferes less with SSEPs and MEPs than volatile agents.

questions.stem: BIS is 15 with burst suppression and hypotension during TIVA. What does this indicate?
options: An artifact from electrocautery near the sensor
questions.explanation: A BIS under 20 is too deep. Reduce the hypnotic and treat hypotension.

questions.stem: A calm awake patient has BIS 95 before induction. How should this be interpreted?
questions.explanation: BIS 90–100 is awake; 40–60 is the general anesthesia target.

questions.stem: The IV site becomes swollen and cool while BIS rises during TIVA. What is the first action?
options: Check for infiltration and restore reliable IV delivery
Increase the propofol rate on the same line to compensate
questions.explanation: Infiltration interrupts drug delivery and causes light anesthesia. Restore reliable IV access first.

questions.stem: When does processed EEG add the most value during TIVA?
options: When clinical assessment of depth is limited
When volatile agents are used at high concentrations
questions.explanation: Processed EEG is an adjunct when depth is hard to judge clinically, as in TIVA with paralysis.

questions.stem: A pump failure goes unnoticed until BIS rises. Which inherent limitation of TIVA contributed?
options: No end-tidal agent concentration to confirm delivery
Slower emergence than volatiles in most patients
questions.explanation: Without end-tidal agent monitoring, TIVA delivery failures may go undetected.

questions.stem: Which THREE practices are essential for safe TIVA when the arms are tucked? (Select 3)
options: Using long extension tubing under drapes
questions.explanation: Accurate programming, visible dedicated lines, and checks for disconnection, occlusion, or infiltration prevent awareness or overdose during TIVA.

questions.stem: A patient with strong family history of malignant hyperthermia requires GA. Which maintenance technique best avoids triggers?
questions.explanation: TIVA avoids triggering agents and is useful when inhaled anesthetics are contraindicated, such as MH susceptibility.

questions.stem: MEPs disappear after rocuronium while SSEPs remain stable. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Neuromuscular blockade abolished the muscle-recorded MEPs
Spinal cord ischemia affecting sensory pathways
Volatile agents depressed the MEPs after the surgeon's request
